red.focus: Understand how Mabo recognized Indigenous native title under Australian law.
red.summary: The Meriam people challenged the assumption that British acquisition of sovereignty erased their traditional land rights. The High Court of Australia recognized native title in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992).
checklist: I can identify the land rights claimed by the Meriam people
I can explain the significance of native title
I can recognize why Mabo did not resolve every Indigenous land claim

sections.title: People already had laws and land
sections.body_md: Eddie Koiki Mabo and other Meriam claimants sought recognition of their people's traditional rights to land on Mer, or Murray Island, in the Torres Strait. They relied on long-standing community laws, customs, and occupation. Earlier colonial legal thinking had often treated the land as lacking owners whose rights the imported legal system needed to recognize. The dispute asked whether Australian common law could acknowledge the Meriam people's existing land rights instead of starting from a fiction that the land belonged to nobody.
sections.audio_script: Eddie Koiki Mabo and other Meriam claimants sought recognition of their people's traditional rights to land on Mer, or Murray Island, in the Torres Strait. They relied on long-standing community laws, customs, and occupation. Earlier colonial legal thinking had often treated the land as lacking owners whose rights the imported legal system needed to recognize. The dispute asked whether Australian common law could acknowledge the Meriam people's existing land rights instead of starting from a fiction that the land belonged to nobody.

sections.title: The High Court recognized native title
sections.body_md: In Mabo v Queensland (No 2), decided June 3, 1992, Australia's High Court held that the common law could recognize native title grounded in the traditional laws and customs of Indigenous peoples. The Meriam people's rights to the relevant lands were recognized subject to specific qualifications. The decision rejected the assumption that Indigenous land rights were necessarily erased when the Crown acquired sovereignty. It did not announce that every parcel of land was automatically transferred or that native title could never be lawfully extinguished.
sections.audio_script: In Mabo v Queensland (No 2), decided June 3, 1992, Australia's High Court held that the common law could recognize native title grounded in the traditional laws and customs of Indigenous peoples. The Meriam people's rights to the relevant lands were recognized subject to specific qualifications. The decision rejected the assumption that Indigenous land rights were necessarily erased when the Crown acquired sovereignty. It did not announce that every parcel of land was automatically transferred or that native title could never be lawfully extinguished.

sections.title: Recognition requires facts and institutions
sections.body_md: Native title claims depend on relevant laws, customs, continuing connections, and the effects of later legally valid acts, among other requirements. The Australian Parliament subsequently enacted the Native Title Act 1993 to provide a statutory framework. A lawyer must not treat Mabo as a universal property deed, yet must also recognize the enormous legal significance of taking Indigenous legal relationships seriously. This is a lesson in how an authoritative court can correct a foundational legal assumption while leaving practical disputes to further processes.

yellow.focus: Explain direct effect through Van Gend en Loos.
yellow.summary: A Dutch importer disputed customs duties under the European Economic Community Treaty. In 1963 the Court of Justice explained that certain treaty rules could create rights enforceable by individuals in national courts.
checklist: I can identify the customs-duty dispute
I can state the central principle of direct effect

sections.title: A company challenged a customs charge
sections.body_md: Van Gend en Loos, a Dutch transport company, was charged duties on chemicals brought from Germany into the Netherlands. It argued that the charge was inconsistent with a rule of the European Economic Community Treaty against increasing certain internal customs duties. The legal question reached the Court of Justice from a national tribunal. Could a company rely on the Treaty rule itself in domestic proceedings, or did only member governments have claims concerning one another's treaty duties?
sections.audio_script: Van Gend en Loos, a Dutch transport company, was charged duties on chemicals brought from Germany into the Netherlands. It argued that the charge was inconsistent with a rule of the European Economic Community Treaty against increasing certain internal customs duties. The legal question reached the Court of Justice from a national tribunal. Could a company rely on the Treaty rule itself in domestic proceedings, or did only member governments have claims concerning one another's treaty duties?

sections.title: The Treaty could create individual rights
sections.body_md: In Van Gend en Loos (Case 26/62, decided February 5, 1963), the Court of Justice held that the Community legal order could confer rights on individuals that national courts must protect. The specific Treaty obligation at issue was suitable for direct effect. The judgment shifted the account of international economic integration away from treating treaties solely as promises between governments. It did not hold that every provision of any international agreement automatically produces a directly enforceable individual right.

sections.title: Test the actual provision
sections.body_md: A lawyer invoking direct effect must identify the relevant European Union rule, whether its terms and legal context satisfy the requirements for enforcement, and who may rely on it against whom. Direct effect differs from choosing a favorable forum or showing that an official behaved unfairly. It concerns whether an authoritative legal norm supplies a right a claimant can invoke in national proceedings. Students should learn the principle without treating an influential founding case as a substitute for contemporary EU doctrine and later qualifications.

orange.focus: Distinguish primacy from direct effect through Costa v ENEL.
orange.summary: In 1964 the Court of Justice considered conflict between Community law and a later Italian national law. Costa developed the principle that Community law could not be displaced simply by a subsequent domestic enactment.
checklist: I can explain why Costa matters for primacy of EU law
I can distinguish primacy from direct effect
I can analyze the relation between national and EU legal orders

sections.title: A national law met an integrated legal order
sections.body_md: Flaminio Costa challenged aspects of an Italian measure nationalizing the electricity industry, raising arguments based on European Economic Community law. The dispute reached the Court of Justice through a preliminary reference from an Italian court. A fundamental question was whether Italy could defeat obligations from the Community legal order simply by adopting a later domestic law. Without an answer, common rules could apply differently in each member state whenever national legislators changed their minds.
sections.audio_script: Flaminio Costa challenged aspects of an Italian measure nationalizing the electricity industry, raising arguments based on European Economic Community law. The dispute reached the Court of Justice through a preliminary reference from an Italian court. A fundamental question was whether Italy could defeat obligations from the Community legal order simply by adopting a later domestic law. Without an answer, common rules could apply differently in each member state whenever national legislators changed their minds.

sections.title: Primacy protects the common rule
sections.body_md: In Costa v ENEL (Case 6/64, decided July 15, 1964), the Court of Justice articulated that law arising from the Community's own legal system could not be overridden by a unilateral subsequent national measure. This became a cornerstone of the doctrine of primacy of EU law. The case did not transfer every area of government to European institutions. EU law's authority remains tied to the Treaties and the legal competences conferred under them, as developed through subsequent doctrine.
sections.audio_script: In Costa v ENEL (Case 6/64, decided July 15, 1964), the Court of Justice articulated that law arising from the Community's own legal system could not be overridden by a unilateral subsequent national measure. This became a cornerstone of the doctrine of primacy of EU law. The case did not transfer every area of government to European institutions. EU law's authority remains tied to the Treaties and the legal competences conferred under them, as developed through subsequent doctrine.

sections.title: Two principles solve different problems
sections.body_md: Van Gend en Loos asks whether a qualifying Community rule can give individuals enforceable rights. Costa asks what priority that legal order has when a national measure conflicts with it. A norm's direct effect and its primacy therefore address distinct questions, even where both matter to a case. An advanced lawyer identifies the applicable EU norm, the claimed inconsistency, the court's available remedy, and the role of later treaty and national constitutional developments. Legal integration does not eliminate interpretive disagreement among courts.

black.focus: Assess constitutional limits on amendment through Kesavananda Bharati.
black.summary: The Indian Supreme Court's 1973 basic-structure doctrine placed limits on the power to alter the Constitution. Compare the protection of constitutional identity with developments in Indigenous recognition and European legal integration.
checklist: I can state the basic-structure principle and its amendment context
I can compare constitutional identity with direct effect and native title
I can critique the legitimacy of protecting essentials against ordinary majorities

sections.title: A constitutional amendment can threaten a constitution
sections.body_md: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973) arose from disputes involving land reform and constitutional amendments in India. A thirteen-judge Supreme Court bench examined Parliament's authority under the Constitution's amendment provisions. By a closely divided result, the Court developed the basic-structure doctrine: Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot destroy its essential structural features. The decision did not say that every constitutional amendment is forbidden or create a simple exhaustive list of all protected features.
sections.audio_script: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973) arose from disputes involving land reform and constitutional amendments in India. A thirteen-judge Supreme Court bench examined Parliament's authority under the Constitution's amendment provisions. By a closely divided result, the Court developed the basic-structure doctrine: Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot destroy its essential structural features. The decision did not say that every constitutional amendment is forbidden or create a simple exhaustive list of all protected features.

sections.title: Different courts reshaped different foundations
sections.body_md: Mabo corrected a colonial assumption about Indigenous land rights. Van Gend en Loos and Costa developed the legal force of a regional legal order within national courts. Kesavananda concerned the internal power to change a written constitution. Each decision transformed a foundational premise, yet the relevant legal source, people protected, and institutional consequences differ. A doctoral comparison should resist calling every landmark decision a rights declaration; some reshape sources, some recognize pre-existing interests, and some limit constituent institutions.

sections.title: Who may decide what cannot be changed?
sections.body_md: Basic-structure limits can protect constitutional democracy against a temporary majority dismantling its safeguards. Critics question whether judges should identify limits not expressly enumerated in the amendment text, potentially restricting democratic reform. A defensible theory must examine institutional history, constitutional interpretation, and the danger of both entrenching injustice and permitting authoritarian change. It should specify how essential features are identified, how courts justify intervention, and how lawful constitutional development remains possible. Legal stability should serve people and freedoms, not merely institutional prestige.
